hints.title: Unique Character Deduction Invariant
hints.text: Certain English number words contain unique identifying letters: z appears only in zero, w only in two, u only in four, x only in six, and g only in eight.

hints.title: Second-Wave Dependency Subtraction
hints.text: After subtracting the counts of even digits, remaining letters uniquely identify odd digits: o identifies one, h identifies three, f identifies five, s identifies seven, i identifies nine.

hints.title: Ascending Sorted Digit Assembly
hints.text: Compute counts for digits 0 through 9 using the two-phase deduction order, then construct the final string by repeating each digit according to its count.

hints.title: See the blueprint
hints.text:
```python
from collections import Counter

class Solution:
    def originalDigits(self, s: str) -> str:
        count = Counter(s)
        out = {}
        out[0] = count["z"]
        out[2] = count["w"]
        out[4] = count["u"]
        out[6] = count["x"]
        out[8] = count["g"]
        out[3] = count["h"] - out[8]
        out[5] = count["f"] - out[4]
        out[7] = count["s"] - out[6]
        out[1] = count["o"] - out[0] - out[2] - out[4]
        out[9] = count["i"] - out[5] - out[6] - out[8]
        res = []
        for d in range(10):
            res.append(str(d) * out[d])
        return "".join(res)
```

complexity.notes: Optimal solution achieving O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Permuting words or backtracking across words produces exponential O(10^(N/4)) runtime.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Counting characters in a single pass of length 26 enables direct algebraic resolution of digit tallies.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Candidate should derive the two-phase dependency order among overlapping English number characters.

class Solution:
    def originalDigits(self, s: str) -> str:
        count = Counter(s)
        out = {}
        out[0] = count["z"]
        out[2] = count["w"]
        out[4] = count["u"]
        out[6] = count["x"]
        out[8] = count["g"]

        out[5] = count["f"] - out[4]
        out[7] = count["s"] - out[6]
        out[1] = count["o"] - out[0] - out[2] - out[4]
        out[9] = count["i"] - out[5] - out[6] - out[8]
        res = []
        for d in range(10):
            res.append(str(d) * out[d])
        return "".join(res)
